item.title: Semi-device-independent channel identification with communication matrices
item.description: arXiv:2511.14273v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We look into the task of differentiating between any two quantum channels and reconstructing them from the obtained measurement statistics with possibly limited information about the experimental set-up. We employ the communication matrix formalism where the measurement statistics of a prepare-and-measure scenario is represented as a stochastic communication matrix. In order to differentiate between any two quantum channels, the informational completeness of the set-up is both necessary and sufficient. On the other hand, if we want to uniquely characterize any quantum channel, in addition we also need to have a complete description of the set-up. We show that in many important cases we can deduce this information directly from the communication matrix of the set-up before applying the channel. Given that we trust the dimension of the system, we show that we can deduce the information completeness of the set-up directly from the rank of the communication matrix. Furthermore, we show that another quantity of the communication matrix, called the information storability, can be used to self-test the set-up (up to an orthogonal transformation) for an important class of states and measurements. This provides us a semi-device-independent way to identify quantum channels from the prepare-and-measure statistics. Lastly, we consider scenarios where we might have some additional information about the channels or additional resources at our disposal which could help us relax some of the assumptions of the proposed scenario.
item.dc:creator: Samgeeth Puliyil, Leevi Lepp\"aj\"arvi, M\'ario Ziman

item.title: Below-shot-noise capacity in phase estimation using nonlinear interferometers
item.description: arXiv:2601.04139v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Over the past decade, several schemes for imaging and sensing based on nonlinear interferometers have been proposed and demonstrated experimentally. These interferometers exhibit two main advantages. First, they enable probing a sample at a chosen wavelength while detecting light at a different wavelength with high efficiency (bicolor quantum imaging and sensing with undetected light). Second, they can show quantum-enhanced sensitivities below the shot-noise limit, potentially reaching Heisenberg-limited precision in parameter estimation. Here, we compare three quantum-imaging configurations using only easily accessible intensity-based measurements for phase estimation: a Yurke-type SU(1,1) interferometer, a Mandel-type induced-coherence interferometer, and a hybrid scheme that continuously interpolates between them. While an ideal Yurke interferometer can exhibit Heisenberg scaling, this advantage is known to be fragile under realistic detection constraints and in the presence of loss. We demonstrate that differential intensity detection in the Mandel interferometer provides the highest and most robust phase sensitivity among the considered schemes, reaching but not surpassing the shot-noise limit, even in the presence of loss. Intensity measurements in a Yurke-type configuration can achieve genuine sub-shot-noise sensitivity under balanced losses and moderate gain; however, their performance degrades in realistic high-gain regimes. Consequently, in this regime, the Mandel configuration with differential detection outperforms the Yurke-type setup and constitutes the most robust approach for phase estimation.
item.dc:creator: Cristofero Oglialoro, Gerard J. Machado, Felix Farsch, Daniel F. Urrego, Alejandra A. Padilla, Raj B. Patel, Ian A. Walmsley, Markus Gr\"afe, Juan P. Torres, Enno Giese

item.title: Interferometric discrepancy between the non-relativistic solution to the Klein-Gordon and Schr\"odinger wave equations due to their dissimilar phase velocities
item.description: arXiv:2601.08007v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adding a constant energy offset leaves classical dynamics unchanged. In quantum mechanics it changes the phase velocity of the wavefunction. The inclusion of the constant rest energy in the Klein-Gordon formulation leads to significantly higher phase velocities compared with the Schr\"odinger equation. The Schr\"odinger equation predicts an attenuation of the wavefunction along one of the paths in a Sagnac interferometer when a beamsplitter's trajectory along that path includes a segment where its speed exceeds the phase velocity of a free particle. Such an attenuation does not occur for electromagnetic waves nor for eigenstates of momentum in the Klein-Gordon equation since the speed of the beamsplitter cannot then exceed the phase velocity of the wave. This attenuation reduces the amplitude without introducing a phase shift, preserving the overall structure of the transmitted wave group. While a Klein-Gordon wave group undergoes three traversals of the beamsplitter that moved, it experiences attenuation equivalent to only a single pass, whereas the Schr\"odinger equation predicts the expected attenuation for three passes. This discrepancy highlights a fundamental incompatibility between the Klein-Gordon equation and the Schr\"odinger equation in a regime where their predictions should converge.
item.dc:creator: Frank Victor Kowalski

item.title: Quantum Recurrent Unit: An Effective and Parameter-Efficient Quantum Neural Network Architecture for NISQ Devices
item.description: arXiv:2601.18164v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid growth of modern machine learning models presents fundamental challenges in parameter efficiency and computational resource requirements. We introduce the Quantum Recurrent Unit (QRU), a novel quantum neural network architecture specifically designed to address these challenges while maintaining compatibility with Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. QRU leverages quantum controlled-SWAP (C-SWAP) gates to implement an information selection mechanism inspired by classical Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), enabling selective processing of temporal information through quantum operations. The architecture features a measurement results feedforward scheme with shared parameters across time steps, achieving a constant parameter count and constant per-step effective quantum circuit depth (the depth of the effectively executed quantum circuit incurred over a single QRU time step) regardless of input sequence length. We validate QRU's performance through three progressive experiments under statevector simulation: oscillatory behavior prediction, high-dimensional feature classification of the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC) dataset, and MNIST handwritten digit classification. Across all tasks, QRU achieves 46.2%-99.7% parameter reduction compared to classical counterparts while achieving comparable performance. Preliminary hardware inference experiments on IBM quantum processors provide initial evidence of execution feasibility on real NISQ devices. The architecture's quantum-native design points toward a candidate quantum-native alternative to classical neural network components, offering a promising direction for parameter-efficient quantum machine learning as hardware capabilities and error mitigation techniques continue to improve.
item.dc:creator: Tzong-Daw Wu, Hsi-Sheng Goan

item.title: Coherent Spin-Photon Interface of Single PL6 Oxygen Vacancy Centers in 4H-SiC
item.description: arXiv:2602.06421v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The oxygen-vacancy PL6 center in 4H-SiC shows a far higher optically detected magnetic resonance contrast than the divacancy, for reasons that have been unclear. Strain-dependent photoluminescence-excitation spectroscopy of single centers yields its excited-state Hamiltonian and state-resolved intersystem-crossing rates, and first-principles calculations trace the enhanced, more spin-selective intersystem crossing to the oxygen-modified excited state. The centers remain photostable under resonant excitation, enabling 99.7\% initialization, coherent optical and spin control, and 5.7~ms coherence.
item.dc:creator: Zhen-Xuan He, Gerg\H{o} Thiering, Xiangru Han, Rui-Jian Liang, Ji-Yang Zhou, Shuo Ren, Wu-Xi Lin, Zhi-He Hao, Qi-Cheng Hu, Jun-Feng Wang, Adam Gali, Jin-Shi Xu, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo

item.title: Flux-Activated Resonant Control of a Bosonic Quantum Memory
item.description: arXiv:2602.18122v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Universal control of bosonic degrees of freedom provides a hardware-efficient route for quantum information processing with high-dimensional systems. Bosonic circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED), which leverages auxillary transmons to coherently control long-lived superconducting cavities, is well suited to this goal. However, such systems are traditionally operated in the dispersive regime, where the nearly degenerate cavity transitions prohibit the direct addressability of individual excitation levels of the bosonic mode and increase gate complexity. Here, we achieve direct oscillator control by dynamically accessing the resonant Jaynes-Cummings (JC) interactions, implemented with a hardware that integrates on-chip broadband magnetic flux delivery with a bosonic memory housed in a 3D superconducting cavity with lifetime exceeding 0.5 ms. We demonstrate deterministic preparation of Fock states and their superpositions within 100s of nanoseconds by directly climbing the JC ladder, and realise efficient arbitrary rotations between a pair of Fock states. Our resonant control scheme provides an analytical method for manipulating the entire Hilbert space of the bosonic mode at rates potentially more favourable than traditional dispersive strategies. This on-demand access to JC interactions serves as a foundational demonstration of an alternative strategy toward realising robust Fock-basis qudits and harnessing the rich dynamics of high-dimensional bosonic systems for quantum information processing.
item.dc:creator: Fernando Valadares, Aleksandr Dorogov, Tanjung Krisnanda, May Chee Loke, Ni-Ni Huang, H\'ector Calero Mas, Seungwon Jin, Pengtao Song, Yvonne Y. Gao

item.title: Programmable quantum simulation of anharmonic dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2603.04744v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In continuous-variable quantum systems, anharmonicity underlies diverse processes such as proton transfer, false vacuum decay and ferroelectric ordering, which cannot arise in a purely harmonic potential. Here, we experimentally demonstrate trigonometric-gate-implemented Fourier synthesis (TGIFS), a compilation scheme for quantum simulation of anharmonic dynamics in continuous-variable-discrete-variable (CV-DV) quantum simulators. TGIFS uses native CV-DV gates, allowing a target anharmonic potential to be determined entirely by classical control parameters, without modification of the hardware. We programmably implement TGIFS with a single trapped ion, simulating coherent dynamics in a continuously tunable family of double-well potentials and synthesising a quartic phase gate. The same circuit structure extends to arbitrary potentials and to multiple modes, giving a route to universal programmable simulation of nonlinearly coupled anharmonic potentials as achievable circuit depth increases.
item.dc:creator: Cameron McGarry, Teerawat Chalermpusitarak, Kai Schwennicke, Frank Scuccimarra, Maverick J. Millican, Vassili G. Matsos, Christophe H. Valahu, Prachi Nagpal, Hon-Kwan Chan, Henry L. Nourse, Ivan Kassal, Ting Rei Tan

item.title: Climbing the Clifford Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2603.12088v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Clifford Hierarchy has been a central topic in quantum computation due to its strong connections with fault-tolerant quantum computation, magic state distillation, and more. Nevertheless, only sections of the hierarchy are fully understood, such as diagonal gates and third level gates. The diagonal part of the hierarchy can be climbed by taking square roots and adding controls. Similarly, square roots of Pauli gates (first level) are Clifford gates (climb to the second level). Based on this theme, we study gates whose square roots climb to the next level. In this paper, we primarily focus on Hermitian gates, and in particular, we fully characterize Hermitian Clifford gates whose square roots climb to the third level.
item.dc:creator: Luca Bastioni, Akash Bhople, Samuel Glandon, Tefjol Pllaha, Madison Stewart, Phillip Waitkevich

item.title: Fulqrum: a generalized framework for quantum subspace diagonalization
item.description: arXiv:2603.18731v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an open-source software framework for computing the solution to Hamiltonian eigenproblems in a subspace defined by bit-strings sampled from a quantum computer. Hamiltonians are represented using an extended alphabet that includes projection and ladder operators, yielding a unified solution method for qubit and fermionic systems. Operators are grouped and sorted so that only non-zero terms need be evaluated and a minimal number of subspace lookup operations performed. Bit-strings are expressed using bit-sets to reduce memory consumption and allow for evaluating operators with no fundamental limit on the number of qubits. Subspaces defined over bit-sets are stored in a hash map format that allows for efficient indexing and lookup operations. Specializations for problems, such as those from quantum chemistry, can further reduce computational costs. Our method can be used to directly construct sparse matrix Hamiltonian representations or obtain matrix-free solutions, allowing users to utilize their eigensolver of choice. We show the benefits of our framework by computing the ground-state solution to examples from condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry with less memory and runtime compared to existing techniques, in some cases by two orders of magnitude or more. This work provides a flexible interface for performant quantum-classical eigensolutions for candidate quantum advantage applications.
item.dc:creator: Paul D. Nation, Abdullah Ash Saki, Hwajung Kang

item.title: Divide-and-Conquer Neural Network Surrogates for Quantum Sampling: Accelerating Markov Chain Monte Carlo in Large-Scale Constrained Optimization Problems
item.description: arXiv:2604.20701v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) [D.~Layden \mbox{\textit{et al.}},\href{https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06095-4} {Nature 619, 282--287 (2023)}] is a promising way to use quantum-circuit samples as MCMC proposals to improve sampling efficiency. On the other hand, many practical problems are large-scale and constrained, making it difficult to construct efficient proposal distributions in classical methods and slowing down MCMC mixing. In this work, we propose a divide-and-conquer neural network surrogate framework for quantum sampling to accelerate MCMC under fixed Hamming weight constraints. Our method divides the interaction graph for an Ising problem into subgraphs, generates samples using QAOA for those subproblems with an XY mixer, and trains neural network surrogates conditioned on the Hamming weight to provide proposal distributions for each subset while preserving the constraint. In numerical experiments of Boltzmann sampling on 3-regular graphs, our method consistently accelerated mixing as the system size $N$ increased, with average improvements in the autocorrelation decay rate constant by speedup factors of about \mbox{$14.0$} and \mbox{$7.7$} over local and global Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. We also applied the method to an MNIST feature mask optimization problem with $N=784$, obtaining faster energy convergence and a classification accuracy 2.03 percentage points higher than that of global Kawasaki dynamics after 50 MCMC steps. These numerical results support the usefulness of surrogate proposals with a divide-and-conquer strategy for large-scale constrained sampling and finite-step optimization.
item.dc:creator: Yuya Kawamata, Yuichiro Nakano, Keisuke Fujii

item.title: Quantum criticality beyond thermodynamic stability
item.description: arXiv:2605.04153v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a many-body system in equilibrium, described by a thermodynamically stable Hamiltonian, quantum criticality is associated with structural changes of the many-body ground state. However, there exist physically relevant models, notably, certain quadratic bosonic Hamiltonians (QBHs), which fail to have a ground state. QBHs can be dynamically stable or unstable. We show the notion of criticality is meaningful for the entire class of QBHs that are dynamically stable or at the boundary of instability, regardless of thermodynamic stability, and that the key state for such QBHs is a naturally and unambiguously defined quasiparticle vacuum (QPV). This state is Gaussian, and coincides with the ground state if the QBH is thermodynamically stable. We identify a relevant spectral gap, the Krein gap, associated to the minimal spectral separation between creation and annihilation operators, and show that the QPV is unique when the Krein gap is positive. We prove that, for dynamically stable QBHs with finite-range couplings, correlations are exponentially bounded unless the Krein gap closes, which is associated with one of two spectral degeneracies: an exceptional point or a Krein collision. Consequently, long-range QPV correlations can ensue. Thus, the Krein gap takes the role of the spectral gap for dynamically stable QBHs, and the boundary of dynamical stability and criticality (associated to exceptional points) or multicriticality (associated to Krein collisions) are the same. We also find that bosonic critical behavior beyond thermodynamic stability is witnessed by the scaling of the entanglement entropy and other indicators of equilibrium criticality from information geometry. Our framework opens the door to investigating all dynamically stable QBHs through the lens of critical phenomena, including thermodynamically unstable ones from photonics, cavity-QED, and magnonics.
item.dc:creator: Mariam Ughrelidze, Vincent P. Flynn, Emilio Cobanera, Lorenza Viola

item.title: CV-QKD over Turbulence Channels with Virtual Photon Subtraction and Quantum Multiple-Symbol Detection for Underwater Quantum Communications
item.description: arXiv:2605.23557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising approach for secure underwater quantum communications (UQCs), where propagation loss, scattering, turbulence, and receiver thermal noise can severely degrade the transmission of quantum states. In this paper, we propose an underwater CV-QKD system with virtual photon subtraction (VPS), implemented through post-selection of Alice's measurement outcomes, without requiring channel state information (CSI) at the receiver. Three VPS-based system configurations are analyzed, corresponding to homodyne detection (VPS-HD), quantum maximum-likelihood detection (VPS-QMLD), and quantum multiple-symbol detection (VPS-QMSD). System performance is evaluated in terms of the accepted-only quantum bit error rate (QBER), where underwater turbulence is modeled by an Erlang distribution. Analytical and semi-closed-form QBER expressions are derived for the three configurations and validated through Monte Carlo simulations for different water types and system parameters. The results show close agreement between analytical and simulation results and demonstrate that VPS-QMSD provides the best robustness against underwater turbulence, achieving the lowest QBER compared with VPS-QMLD and VPS-HD.
item.dc:creator: Nour Rizk, Hesham S. Ibrahim, Ang\'elique Dr\'emeau, Arnaud Coatanhay

item.title: Causal Order Cannot Be An Observable
item.description: arXiv:2605.25302v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent developments in the formalisation of quantum causal structures have made it possible to test and compare hypotheses about causal structure empirically, rather than being a-priori assumptions. Such differences in causal structure may be leveraged to distinguish between the processes they belong to, akin to distinguishing between quantum states known to belong to different eigenspaces of an observable. So how far this analogy can be pushed? Can causal order be interpreted as a kind of observable? Can it be measured? To this end we construct a completely operational definition of observables in terms of `discrimination tasks'. This begins with some base set of classes (analogous to a quantum observable's eigenspaces) before we impose three conditions on how these classes relate under discrimination tasks. These conditions recover the properties of a standard observable, letting us apply this definition to non-state entities such as quantum processes, which naturally encode causal structure. The first of these conditions (1) asserts that a member of any class is perfectly distinguishable from a member of any other class -- for states, this implies conditions (2) and (3), but we show this does not hold automatically for processes (or indeed channels). By analysing classes of quantum processes having strict causal orders, we find causal classes which are sharp but violate condition 2 (but not 3), and classes which are likewise sharp and violate condition 3 (but not 2). This implies that causal order cannot be an observable.

item.dc:creator: Declan Maguire, Fabio Costa

item.title: Modular non-Hermitian topology and its application to critical sensing
item.description: arXiv:2605.29173v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Non-Hermitian topological systems have attracted a lot of research activities in recent times, both theoretically and experimentally, due to their unique physical properties and association with open quantum systems. We show that modular structures, where specific couplings at regular intervals take distinct values, enrich the unique topological attributes of these systems such as the non-Hermitian skin effect and the breakdown of conventional bulk-boundary correspondence. These systems also possess the capability of displaying criticality-enhanced sensitivity for precision metrology. We establish how the modular structure, in suitable parameter regime, enhances their sensing performance near spectral topological phase transitions and show that the enhancement can be achieved in multi-parameter estimation scenarios as well.
item.dc:creator: Saubhik Sarkar, Chiranjib Mukhopadhyay, Abolfazl Bayat

item.title: Semidefinite-programming hierarchies for classically simulable state sets
item.description: arXiv:2606.06204v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Determining whether a quantum state set admits a classical explanation is a fundamental problem in quantum information theory, as it reveals whether the information encoded in state preparation can be reproduced by classical means. Here we study classically simulable state sets, namely those admitting realizations using shared randomness and preparation devices that individually generate only pairwise commuting state sets. We develop a complete semidefinite programming (SDP) hierarchy to characterize the set of classically simulable state sets. The key step is a reformulation of classical simulability as a feasibility problem involving deterministic response functions and auxiliary positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs) simulable by rank-one projective measurements. We then establish a complete SDP hierarchy for rank-one projectively simulable POVMs, which in turn induces computable outer approximations converging to the set of classically simulable state sets. The corresponding dual SDP further yields affine witnesses that can be used to rule out classical simulability. Applying the hierarchy to state sets under depolarizing noise yields computable upper bounds on the critical visibility. For several highly symmetric examples, these bounds are matched by explicit classical simulations, providing evidence for the practical usefulness of the hierarchy.
item.dc:creator: Mengyan Li, Yanning Jia, Fenzhuo Guo, Haifeng Dong, Sujuan Qin, Fei Gao

item.title: Pauli-Z Moment Matrices in the Variational Quantum Power Method: Goemans-Williamson Rounding, Qubit Locking, and a Correlation-Based Circuit-Cutting Heuristic
item.description: arXiv:2606.23727v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The matrix of single- and two-qubit Pauli-Z expectation values of any quantum state is the moment matrix of its computational-basis outcome distribution; it therefore lies in the cut polytope and, in particular, is a feasible point of the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (Goemans-Williamson, GW) relaxation. Applying GW random-hyperplane rounding to this matrix yields cuts of expected weight at least alpha_GW times the state's energy. This observation and the resulting bound are not new: the bound is the GW inequality applied to the circuit's covariance matrix, and it was stated and used in exactly this form by Martinez, Fawzi and Stilck Franca, who interpret it as showing that a classical surrogate nearly reproduces the circuit and add noisy-circuit guarantees and hardware experiments; relax-and-round of QAOA correlation matrices, with spectral rather than hyperplane rounding, was introduced earlier by Dupont and Sundar. The bound is also not stronger than what direct computational-basis sampling of the state already gives in expectation. In this note we revisit the bound as a post-processing of the two-point data produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA and the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), and give an energy-leakage bound for VQPM qubit locking. We further discuss a heuristic that uses the connected Z-correlation matrix to propose candidate qubit bipartitions for circuit cutting, in the spirit of existing correlation- and mutual-information-based partitioning methods, together with product-state error bounds in terms of quantum mutual information. Pairwise Z-correlations neither certify product structure of the state nor factorization of the underlying unitary, and the error bounds require quantities not available from Z-data alone.
item.dc:creator: Ammar Daskin

item.title: Reducing quantum measurements in qubit-based overlapping grouping methods for quantum energy estimation through better initializations
item.description: arXiv:2607.02794v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The measurement cost for estimating expectation values of Hamiltonians is a central bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms. Grouping strategies significantly reduce this cost, with overlapping techniques as the state of the art. Overlapping grouping methods require i) a non-overlapping grouping of the Hamiltonian, typically obtained from the Sorted Insertion (SI) algorithm as initialization, and ii) the construction of covariance dictionaries from approximate wavefunctions to guide the optimization. It was recently shown that different initializations can potentially reduce measurement costs for overlapping methods. Motivated by these findings, we introduce variance-aware SI (VarSI), a family of covariance-informed non-overlapping Pauli grouping heuristics to reduce measurement counts. VarSI grouping leverages the covariance dictionaries, already required by overlapping methods, to construct better non-overlapping groups. We propose three variants: a global greedy grouping insertion rule, a variance-informed SI analog, and a local refinement step initialized from SI or our variance-informed variant. We showcase the use of the VarSI groupings as initialization of overlapping methods using the iterative coefficient-splitting (ICS) algorithm. Molecular benchmarks with 130 Hamiltonians demonstrate consistent, non-overlapping measurement improvements over SI of 36--39\% and enhanced downstream ICS results when initialized from VarSI groups. We find that the initializations considered here achieve larger reductions of up to 48\% for systems whose covariances deviate from idealized cases. Compared to the standard SI initialization, VarSI reaches mean reductions of 10.3--13.5\% depending on qubit mappings and covariance dictionaries used. These results show that non-overlapping grouping remains a consequential design step even when the final estimator uses overlapping fragments.
item.dc:creator: Isaac L. Huidobro-Meezs, Rodrigo A. Vargas-Hern\'andez

item.title: Quantum Oracle Value Readout: Coherence, Complementarity, and Fragility
item.description: arXiv:2607.13198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A response-register quantum oracle can reveal a function value or encode it as a phase through kickback. We quantify how much value information can be recovered from one query at a fixed fidelity to a target phase character, and how noise and implementation errors affect readout performance. For pure response states over finite Abelian groups, the known covariant discrimination solution fixes the optimal readout probability exactly in terms of the $\ell_1$-norm coherence of the response state in the character basis. Using a known coherence bound, we determine the complete pure-state readout interval at fixed target-character fidelity. Discarding the response leaves a mixture of phase-oracle channels whose distance from the target, measured by half the diamond norm, is at most the target-character infidelity, with equality for surjective functions. We then identify when coherence alone determines performance and when apparatus correlations or loss profiles are also needed. For coherent analyzer errors, we derive the full quadratic loss and an exact scalar reduction of the profile model on the upper phase--value boundary. For mode-dependent loss, no-detection events can carry value information, and a universal bound is attained under a phase--loss compatibility condition. Photonic-mesh simulations test the analyzer-error predictions, with the controlled oracle itself assumed. Selected results extend to finite non-Abelian groups, where scalar phase kickback is restricted to one-dimensional representations.
item.dc:creator: Milad Ghadimi, Hesam Soltanpanahi, Vahid Salari, Mariam Zomorodi

item.title: How many degrees of freedom describe a quantum N-particle state?
item.description: arXiv:2607.16988v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In Newtonian spacetime, the canonical description of a classical $N$-particle system requires $3N$ degrees of freedom. Not all of these are physical, however, since the conservation of the net momentum implies that only $3(N-1)$ accelerations are independent. Hence, three constraints can be used to eliminate the unphysical centre-of-mass variables, at the level of the Lagrangian, leaving only the subset of observable displacements and momenta, which are relational. Imposing the constraints does not change the dynamics of these variables, at the classical level, and is analogous to a gauge-fixing procedure, which removes redundancy in the description of the system. In classical physics, therefore, the number of physical degrees of freedom equals the number of independent relational degrees of freedom. Here, we show that this is not the case in quantum mechanics. While an operator-analogue of the classical net momentum exists, it cannot be used to impose constraints that restrict the degrees of freedom in the theory, without a loss of physical information. This means that all $3N$ canonical degrees of freedom are physical, even though only $3(N-1)$ of them are relational. We explore the physical consequences of the non-relational variables and show that they give rise to generalised uncertainty relations (GURs), for the relational quantities that define the quantum reference frame (QRF). Hence, it is shown that the non-relational degrees of freedom refer to the frame itself and that the non-Heisenberg terms in the GURs define its Galilean-invariant spreads, in both real space and momentum space. The implications of this result for recent work on relational models, including the ``perspective neutral'' framework for QRFs, are discussed. Its implications for the wider relational program, and, in particular, the relevance of the latter to quantum gravity research, are also critically assessed
item.dc:creator: Matthew J. Lake, Marek L. Miller

item.title: Detecting quantum phase transitions via shallow variational quantum circuits
item.description: arXiv:2607.25345v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mapping quantum phase diagrams through classical simulation is notoriously resource-intensive, as even small systems far from the thermodynamic limit demand prohibitive computational effort. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) offers a compelling alternative, exploiting approximate ground states to distinguish phases. An appealing proposal, dubbed as Delta-VQE, determines critical points by contrasting variational energies optimized from reference states of distinct phases. Intriguingly, the diagnostic sharpens as circuit depth decreases, highlighting its promise as a resource-conscious probe of quantum criticality. To probe the broader applicability and underlying mechanisms of this approach, we investigate the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model with a three-spin cluster interaction, a setting in which the Ising transitions are generally situated beyond the self-dual line. We demonstrate that, whenever dual ans\"atze are employed, Delta-VQE invariably detects the self-dual points rather than the true criticality. In contrast, when ans\"atze are carefully tailored to embody the competing phases across the boundary, the genuine Ising critical point can be successfully identified with only minor finite-size effects. Our results establish that, while Delta-VQE provides a resource-efficient probe of quantum criticality without requiring precise ground-state preparation, its diagnostic power is fundamentally contingent upon the judicious selection of physically representative ans\"atze.
item.dc:creator: Ching-Yu Huang, Min-Fong Yang

item.title: Single-molecule strong optomechanical regimes in SERS via hybrid plasmonic cavities
item.description: arXiv:2608.03307v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We identify enhanced strong coherent Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS) interactions facilitated by hybridized metallo-dielectric cavities with a resonant fluorescent molecule. By illuminating a detuned electronic transition near saturation via a narrowband hybrid plasmonic mode, we observe enhanced splittings in the Stokes and anti-Stokes spectra, revealing strong optomechanical coupling and nonlinear vibrational modifications at intensities far below irreversible SERS damage thresholds. We compute the second-order photon correlations that allows identifying the nonclassical character associated to these strong optomechanical interactions and SERS configurations that enables them to optically characterize the anharmonic character of the vibrational modes.
item.dc:creator: Miguel \'A. Mart\'inez-Garc\'ia, Johannes Feist, Diego Mart\'in-Cano

item.title: Millisecond optical coherence and strong collective coupling in an integrated telecom rare-earth photonic platform
item.description: arXiv:2608.08221v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-range quantum network nodes require the combination of strong light-matter coupling, long coherence times and in-situ spectral control at telecom wavelengths. The coherence of erbium in integrated devices is held back by its hosts, which do not simultaneously provide the weakly magnetic nuclear-spin environment and the well-defined substitutional sites found in coherence-optimised bulk crystals. Here we bring such an optimised crystal onto a photonic chip, by bonding an Er${^{3+}}$:CaWO${_{4}}$ host without an adhesive interlayer to a high-${Q}$ electro-optically tuneable thin-film lithium niobate microring resonator. At an effective temperature of 75mK and a field of only 0.2T, ions probed through a waveguide show an effective homogeneous linewidth of ${289\pm5}$Hz (${T_{\text{M}}=1.10\pm0.02}$ms), with spectral diffusion proceeding at ${86\pm18}$Hz and saturating at ${1.5\pm0.2}$kHz. Electro-optically tuning the resonator through the erbium optical transition resolves an avoided crossing with a collective cooperativity of ${C=6.7\pm0.4}$ at zero field and ${C=4.9\pm0.2}$ at 0.4T, where ${T_{\text{M}}}$ exceeds 1ms. Exploiting superhyperfine coupling to the host's ${^{183}}$W nuclear spins, we store and retrieve optical phase information over 5s with a visibility of ${0.935\pm0.015}$. Strong collective coupling, millisecond coherence and in-situ spectral tuning in a single device thus establish heterogeneous integration leveraging coherence-optimised hosts as a route to scalable telecom quantum networks.
item.dc:creator: Kah Jen Wo, Pavel A. Dmitriev, Karthik Dasigi, Fumiya Hanamura, Steven Touzard

item.title: Divergence between Maximum-Probability and Maximum-Likelihood Decoding in the Low-Noise Limit of Quantum Error Correction
item.description: arXiv:2608.18420v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the asymptotic low-noise limit of quantum error correction, two optimal decoding rules can disagree. Maximum-probability (MP) decoding selects the most probable microscopic error, whereas degenerate maximum-likelihood (MLD) decoding selects the logical sector with the largest total probability. Under code-capacity Pauli noise, we determine the first physical error weight $m$ at which the MP and MLD logical winner sets become provably disjoint, even under optimal MP tie resolution. As the physical error rate tends to zero, MLD retains a residual zero-temperature degeneracy from the multiplicity of minimum-weight errors sharing a syndrome and logical label, which can outweigh the single most probable error. Code distance imposes the universal bound $m\geq h=\lceil d/2\rceil$; the rigidity depth $r$, defined by $m=h+r$, counts the additional error-weight shells above $h$ on which MP and MLD remain equivalent. We certify a three-level hierarchy: $r=0$ for planar surface codes and two recursively concatenated families, $r=1$ for odd-distance square toric codes and the Gross $[[144,12,12]]$ quantum low-density-parity-check code, and $r=2$ for a separable family with hypergraph product and bivariate bicycle descriptions. The onset weight fixes the leading failure-rate gap between best-tie MP and MLD, proportional to the $m$th power of the physical noise strength, providing an exact subthreshold benchmark for the advantage of degeneracy-aware decoding over the computationally cheaper nondegenerate rule.
item.dc:creator: Yixin Zhao, Fei Yan

item.title: Entanglement and magic transitions in an all-to-all non-Hermitian spin model
item.description: arXiv:2608.31064v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The long-time state of a non-Hermitian system is determined by the eigenvalue with the largest imaginary part. In interacting many-body systems this eigenvalue usually cannot be tracked analytically, and the character of the state it selects is unknown. We construct a non-Hermitian spin ensemble of $L$ spins with exactly $k$-local all-to-all interactions, in which this dominant eigenvalue can be tracked analytically from the clean limit into the disordered regime. Disorder produces a competition between an isolated spectral outlier and the edge of a many-body spectral bulk. We study three cases: purely anti-Hermitian disorder, purely Hermitian disorder, and mixed disorder of equal strength. For purely anti-Hermitian and mixed disorder, we show that when the bulk overtakes the outlier in imaginary part, the dominant eigenstate switches from an outlier state with low entanglement and magic (nonstabilizerness) to a bulk state with substantially larger entanglement and magic, with both changing at the same threshold. For $k \gg \sqrt{L}$ the bulk has a sharp spectral edge and the transition thresholds follow in closed form, while for $k \ll \sqrt{L}$ spectral tails broaden the transition into a crossover. Purely Hermitian disorder provides a contrasting case with no outlier-to-bulk switching. Finally, we map the non-Hermitian evolution exactly onto postselected trajectories of a monitored quantum system, connecting this spectral mechanism to measurement-induced transitions.
item.dc:creator: Sasanka Dowarah, Michael Kolodrubetz

item.title: Asymmetric quantum error correction efficiently tackles application-specific noise effects
item.description: arXiv:2609.07235v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Noise is a major challenge for current quantum computers. It can be broadly categorized into bit-flip and phase-flip errors. These two types do not necessarily affect the executed algorithm, thus also the application, in the same way. We illustrate this general effect for the example of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to a small instance of the flight-gate assignment (FGA) problem. We compare bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise under both layer-level and gate-level noise models, using two circuit decompositions of the same ideal QAOA unitary: a CNOT-based decomposition and a native-RZZ decomposition. For the six-qubit FGA instance considered here, bit-flip noise produces a larger degradation in the optimized QAOA performance across the investigated circuit depths and noise models. The asymmetry is most pronounced in the layer-level and native-RZZ simulations. We explain this behavior through the commutation and propagation properties of the errors and their effects on the final computational-basis measurements. Since these mechanisms are not specific to the considered FGA instance, we expect similar noise asymmetries to arise in other Ising-based QAOA applications, although this remains to be investigated. We then exploit these insights to tackle noise particularly efficiently using asymmetric error-correcting codes. As an illustration, we use the quantum parity code (QPC), a generalization of the 9-qubit Shor code, and show that a smaller asymmetric code can achieve nearly the same improvement as a larger symmetric choice. This suggests that allocating error-correction resources according to algorithmic noise sensitivity, rather than physical error rates alone, can be beneficial even when the physical noise is symmetric. Finally, we discuss how information about the noise obtained through calibration can be exploited in our approach.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Yadav, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Michael Epping

item.title: Parallel and Distributed Fermionic Simulation via Dynamic Encoding
item.description: arXiv:2609.31502v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We demonstrate a simple and efficient method to parallelize and distribute Trotterized Hamiltonian simulation of fermionic systems across multiple QPUs. Using combinatorial covering designs to define a fixed set of fermion-qubit encodings, independent of system size, we demonstrate communication cost scaling as $\mathcal{O}(M q^3 r)$ for a system of $M$ fermionic modes and Trotter number $r$. This improves on the static encoding bound for $q$ QPUs, $\mathcal{O}(M^4 q r)$. In terms of QPU register size $R$, at most $R^{1/3}$ QPUs are able to parallelize at most $R^{4/3}$ fermionic modes. We compare this approach to dynamic encoding using a randomized method, Pauli-weight based optimization and hypergraph partitioning. Applying these to the Hamiltonians of a range of molecular systems split across two and three QPUs, we find the combinatorial covering approach results in significantly reduced communication cost.
item.dc:creator: Michael Williams de la Bastida, Peter V. Coveney

item.title: Optimal GHZ extraction from MABK violations
item.description: arXiv:2610.08516v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that, for $n\geq3$ parties, the minimum Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) extractability at normalized Mermin-Ardehali-Belinskii-Klyshko (MABK) score $t\in[0,1]$ is $(1+t)/2$ over all states and binary measurements, allowing arbitrary local dimensions. The extractability $\Xi_n(\rho)$ of a state $\rho$ is the supremum of squared GHZ overlap over local channels. The score $t$ scales linearly from zero at the biseparable bound to one at the quantum maximum. This recovers the three- to five-party bounds and proves the conjecture of Cao et al. for $n\geq6$. We determine the exact qubit minimum, strictly higher for $0<t<1$. We construct a mixture on one qutrit and $n-1$ qubits attaining the bound with fixed measurements and score-dependent weights. We prove that at interior scores it has the smallest product of local ranks among attaining states, $3\cdot2^{n-1}$, and for $n\geq4$ is unique at that product up to local isometries and party permutations. With one qutrit, $n-1$ qubits and arbitrary binary measurements, set $\varepsilon:=\Xi_n(\rho)-(1+t)/2$. For $n\geq4$, $t$ bounded away from zero and small $\varepsilon$, we prove that the state's trace-norm distance to the mixture at score $t$, up to local unitaries, is $O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$, uniformly in $n$ with optimal exponent. For $n=3$ we bound this distance explicitly above $t_0\approx0.69333$. For $n\geq3$ and $t>0$, we bound this distance from the Bell score and the expectations of five calibrated binary qutrit measurements, given the local dimensions and a known two-dimensional qutrit subspace invariant under both qutrit Bell observables.
item.dc:creator: Avraham Kreindel (Yohananov), Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy (Yohananov)

item.title: Low-field dephasing time of an optically polarized NV$^-$ spin bath beyond the P1 limit in diamond: a cluster-correlation-expansion and exact spin-bath study
item.description: arXiv:2610.29279v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dense ensembles of nitrogen-vacancy (NV$^-$) centres in nitrogen-rich diamond dephase on the electron spins of the substitutional nitrogen (P1) centres. If the paramagnetic nitrogen is instead converted into NV$^-$ centres, the laser that initializes the sensor also pumps the bath into $m_s = 0$, a state with no moment along its own axis. Using cluster-correlation-expansion (CCE) calculations with a dynamical mean field, combined with an exact solver for probe-bath exchange and with no adjustable parameter, this paper asks whether such an optically polarized NV$^-$ bath dephases a sensor more slowly than a P1 bath of the same density. The answer is set by the field. In a field along [111], three quarters of the bath centres lie off the field axis, and the moment of their $m_s = 0$ state along the field grows from 0.04 at 25 G to 0.46 at 300 G and 0.81 at 800 G. At 25 G the polarized bath is therefore nearly silent: at 0.57 ppm the dephasing time $T_2^*$ of a separately addressed $^{15}$NV$^-$ probe is 112 $\mu$s, six times the 18.0 $\mu$s of a P1 bath, and still 2.4 times at 90% polarization; an ensemble measurement gains a factor of two. At 300 G the advantage over P1 shrinks to 1.4, and at 800 G the polarized bath dephases faster than P1. The field dependence of every bath, P1 included, follows the mean moment of its centres along the field. For the Hahn echo, bath relaxation ($T_1$ = 6 ms) caps the gain: a $^{15}$NV$^-$ probe in a polarized bath reaches 1.5 times the P1 value at 25 G and 1.14-1.16 times at 300 and 800 G. Optical polarization of an NV$^-$ bath at low field therefore offers dephasing times beyond the P1 limit of nitrogen-rich diamond.
item.dc:creator: Chikara Shinei

item.title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.32605v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present QuantumBilliards.jl, an open-source Julia library providing a suite of numerical solvers for the two-dimensional interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos. The library implements conventional wavenumber-sweep techniques together with several accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini--Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a common framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, and treating smooth, cornered, and multiply connected domains. The library further includes reconstruction of eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives and the computation of Poincar\'e--Husimi (PH) phase-space representations. Available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Chaos-Julia/QuantumBilliards.jl.
item.dc:creator: Matic Orel, \v{C}rt Lozej

item.title: Are quantum measurements universal?
item.description: arXiv:2610.37873v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In 2014, with D. Aerts, we showed, in the extended Bloch representation of quantum mechanics, that the Born rule results from a universal average over all the ways the measurement-interaction can be selected, computed by averaging over discretized (cellular) densities and taking a continuum limit. N. Shackel has since criticized this construction, in the context of Bertrand's paradox, for depending on the discretization adopted, for the constancy of its averages, and for the unclear sense in which the average is over 'all' densities. His criticisms prompt the present re-examination. What makes a random way of selecting a measurement 'universal', we argue, is that it privileges no portion of the structure of the available interactions, a property we call indifference and adopt as definitional. We prove that every universal measurement, however constructed, produces exactly the Born probabilities: the universal average is unique, the 2014 construction is one realization among infinitely many, and for cellular measurements the result is exact at every finite resolution, with no limit to be taken, which explains the constancy of the averages. Non-trivial universal measurements exist, but must involve deterministic measurements: Dirichlet processes are universal measurements whose support contains every way of selecting an interaction, whereas one free of deterministic components selects the uniform density, so that for it the Born rule holds with certainty, not merely on average. In sequences of measurements, deterministic components produce deviations from quantum statistics governed by a single parameter, in principle accessible to experiment. The only geometric input is the Euclidean length of the membrane and the orthogonal landing of the point-particle, where Gleason's theorem enters. We indicate the generalization to any number of outcomes and the bearing on Bertrand's paradox.
item.dc:creator: Massimiliano Sassoli de Bianchi

item.title: Distributed Inner-Product Estimation for Continuous-Variable Quantum States
item.description: arXiv:2610.40141v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distributed inner-product estimation (DIPE) is a fundamental task in quantum information, aiming to estimate the inner product between two unknown quantum states prepared on separate quantum platforms. In multimode continuous-variable (CV) systems, the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space poses additional challenges. In this work, we propose a protocol for CV-DIPE that requires the two platforms to share a common phase reference and perform local homodyne measurements at the same randomly sampled phase settings, followed by classical post-processing of the measurement data. We derive explicit upper bounds on the sample complexity of this protocol. These bounds depend on the available physical prior information. Specifically, we provide bounds for two natural cases: finite-energy states and Gaussian states. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the theoretical performance of this estimation scheme. Our findings offer a CV-DIPE protocol that relies solely on homodyne measurements and remains applicable even when neither of the two quantum states is fully characterized.
item.dc:creator: Jun Tang, Congcong Zheng, Yujie Miao, Xutao Yu, Zaichen Zhang

item.title: Toric codes all the way down: decoupling translation-invariant topological CSS codes in higher dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2610.40592v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes in more than two spatial dimensions offer features useful for fault-tolerant quantum computation, such as transversal non-Clifford gates and single-shot decoding, but a systematic understanding of them is still lacking. One approach is to decouple a code: map it to a stack of higher-form toric codes by a finite-depth local CSS-preserving Clifford circuit, possibly after adding ancillas. For translation-invariant $p$-ary CSS codes, where $p$ is prime ($p=2$ for qubits), we require the circuit to commute with the translations of a superlattice. In two dimensions, such a decoupling exists once these translations act trivially on every anyon type. In higher dimensions, excitations are sorted by their dimension into superselection layers, which can remain glued together even when translations act trivially on each layer. We show that this gluing is the only remaining obstruction: a code can be decoupled on a superlattice exactly when, after coarse-graining to it, translations act trivially on every layer and the gluing vanishes. Moreover, for a code with finitely many excitation types in each layer and $m$ nonzero layers, once translations act trivially on every layer, further coarse-graining by a factor of $p^{m-1}$ in every direction removes the aforementioned gluing. Physically, the same criterion determines when the code encodes the maximal number of logical qudits on a finite torus. Finally, we give an explicit algorithm that constructs the decoupling as a circuit of SUM (qudit CNOT) and SWAP gates.
item.dc:creator: Mingxin He, Yifei Wang, Hao Song, Yingfei Gu

item.title: Dynamical-mean-field cluster-correlation expansion of NV$^-$ spin-echo decoherence in a realistic substitutional-nitrogen bath
item.description: arXiv:2611.02528v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Hahn-echo time $T_2$ of nitrogen-vacancy (NV$^-$) ensembles in nitrogen-rich diamond follows the empirical relation $T_2\cdot$[N] = 160 $\mu$s ppm, and this relation does not depend on the magnetic field between 2 and 30 mT. Cluster-correlation-expansion (CCE) calculations solve the spin dynamics exactly within small groups of spins. When they treat the Overhauser field of the surrounding P1 centres, that is, the field that these electron spins produce, as frozen, they overestimate $T_2$ at high field by up to a factor of two. This excess was recently attributed to additional dark defects. We show that the excess comes mostly from the frozen field. In our model the P1 centres outside each cluster flip-flop in pairs: two centres exchange their spin states and conserve their total $S_z$. Kinetic Monte Carlo generates these events at golden-rule rates, which follow from the dipolar Hamiltonian without adjustable parameters, and each cluster evolves in the resulting time-dependent field. This dynamical mean field lies between the static-mean-field and mean-field-free limits. For a $^{14}$N P1 bath it reduces $T_2\cdot$[N] at 30 mT from 264 $\pm$ 16 to 188 $\pm$ 12 $\mu$s ppm and gives 167 $\pm$ 11 $\mu$s ppm at 10 mT, 1.7 and 0.4 standard deviations from experiment, with no dark spins. When each centre jumps independently, $T_2\cdot$[N] is 147 $\pm$ 9 $\mu$s ppm at 30 mT; the correlation of the flip-flop partners thus lengthens $T_2$ by 20-30 percent at high field. The Overhauser field is neither frozen nor averaged out by fast motion: 68-83 percent of its autocorrelation survives 200 $\mu$s. At 2.5 mT, where the P1 electron and nucleus hybridise, $T_2$ stays below experiment for any choice of rates. Part of the field dependence therefore remains: $T_2$ rises by a factor 1.69 $\pm$ 0.07 instead of 2.15 $\pm$ 0.08 from 2.5 to 30 mT.
item.dc:creator: Chikara Shinei

item.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2611.05355v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection (an interference, a balanced interferometric reading or a camera) and the output is a Born probability: attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^2$, the form of the Born rule, normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections a classical controller squares, divides, rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-13}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference the model reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % test accuracy, level within the spread of three seeds with a softmax transformer of the same size (76.62 +- 0.36 %). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of test pairs, out of the 53 % any single deletion can change, against 32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients and 31 % for the Born Transformer's own attention. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics (simulated), and its attention overlaps to Hadamard tests on qubits; a separate coherent attention layer becomes one post-selected circuit (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps, the device gave the model's answers on the two shortest test pairs, also when the one word that decides one of them was deleted; with calibration circuits as deep as the overlaps, each word's evidence with the device's attention row sums followed the exact evidence on one pair (correlation 0.997) and on the other less closely (0.962).
item.dc:creator: Teerawat Tongloy, Jiraporn Pongsopa, Rangsan Jomtarak

item.title: Optimal finite-copy readout of three-qubit entanglement with state retention
item.description: arXiv:2611.08233v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For unknown three-qubit pure states, we characterize the optimal trade-off among GHZ-class certification, binary probability readout of the three-tangle, and conditional state retention. The vanishing ideal of the null class specifies the optimal certification subspace, while a polynomial multiplication operator gives the spectral limit for binary readout. Four copies are necessary for a nonzero certificate. A fifth copy raises the optimal success probability from $\tau^{2}/48$ to $5\tau^{2}/72$ and permits the original unknown state to be retained, where $\tau$ is the three-tangle. We obtain this gain as an instance of a general symmetry-based additional-copy theorem. At six copies the optimal certification probability is $(39+2S)\tau^{2}/296$, with $S=\sum_{X}\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho_{X}^{2}$, whereas the largest exact binary probability is $\tau^{2}/8$. Local Schur measurements and conditional local operations with classical communication attain these bounds. Retaining the full six-copy branch record yields a weighted estimator with lower variance than binary thinning of the same data. Explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons connect the success probabilities to input-copy consumption, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Xin Wu, Yuan-Hong Tao, Ji-Hui Mo, Peng-Fei Ma, Shu-Hui Wu, Shao-Ming Fei

item.title: Random encoders and expurgation improve 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
item.description: arXiv:2611.08744v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I report 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes $[[n,k,d]]$ with $53\le n\le 254$ and $5\le d\le 13$ whose minimum distance exceeds the lower bound listed in Grassl's code tables at the same $(n,k)$: 161 codes by one and 31 by two. Through the standard propagation rules they raise 1,873 entries of the table. For 190 of the codes, a random Clifford encoder is followed by expurgation: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few logical operators are promoted to stabilizers so that each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one of them. The other two are obtained by puncturing a code from the table and repairing it in the same way. All 192 distances are exact: the lower bound is certified by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle enumeration of up to $4\times10^{13}$ Pauli operators, and the upper bound by an explicit logical operator of weight $d$. A first-moment count explains the results. Expurgated random codes have about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, so they beat the table wherever its best known codes are no better than random. The largest gains, up to nine logical qubits, are at $d\ge9$ and $n\gtrsim170$, where the table often gives a lower bound without an explicit code. The same count predicts improvements at 619 further pairs $(n,d)$. The search was run by AI agents. The codes, their certificates and an independent checker are public.
item.dc:creator: Marin Girard

item.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
item.description: arXiv:2611.10529v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.
item.dc:creator: Sanim Yousuf Fahim, Mohammad Arif Hossain

item.title: Hidden Coherence and Controlled Quasihole Motion in a Fermionic Laughlin State on a Superconducting Quantum Processor
item.description: arXiv:2611.10687v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states support fractionalized excitations and geometric phases, yet experimentally resolving the many-body coherence encoded in their wave functions remains challenging. Here, we prepare a three-electron $\nu=1/3$ Laughlin state on the Haldane sphere using seven superconducting qubits and reconstruct its many-body density matrix. Through Read's composite-boson construction, we reveal vortex-dressed coherence that remains appreciable over a larger separation range than electron coherence. The extended profile is suppressed in a Fock-diagonal reference constructed from the measured populations, demonstrating its dependence on off-diagonal many-body coherence. We further prepare a one-flux-added quasihole and characterize its fractional charge response against finite-size benchmarks. Controlled quasihole motion yields an effective geometric-phase signature from the reconstructed dominant-eigenstate trajectory. These complementary measurements provide microscopic access to the coherent structure and quasihole response of a finite fermionic Laughlin state, demonstrating an experimental route to probing strongly correlated FQH wave functions on programmable quantum processors.
